title: Neuronal activity-driven 3D chromatin dynamics in cortical pyramidal neurons depend on SATB2.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed all 9 deposited processed BED files from GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) FTP. Counted rows: open chromatin regions (OCRs) in control (floxed) neurons 13,573 gained / 550 lost / 109,573 invariant; in Satb2 knockout 1,569 gained / 11,825 lost / 104,755 invariant; SATB2 protein-binding peaks 4,552 gained / 2,042 lost / 11,068 invariant. Checked widths (gained median 360 bp, invariant 537 bp), zero duplicate coordinates, zero overlap between gained and invariant sets, 24 chromosomes. Computed the key join myself: 5,923 of 13,573 gained OCRs overlap a knockout-lost region. Also opened the RNA-seq count table (56,422 genes x 16 samples) and the Zenodo code archive (1.7 MB, scripts only). Checked Hi-C file sizes by HEAD request (20-21 GB each).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Genome build mm10 and the peak-calling recipe (MACS3 on replicate-merged BAM files, Bic-treated as treatment vs NBQX-treated as control, p<1e-12) are in the Methods, not in the files. Motif enrichment for MEF2/FOS/JUNB/FOSL2/NPAS4 at gained OCRs is from the paper's Supplementary Table S1, which I did not retrieve (Europe PMC supplementary endpoint timed out). The 1,165 activity-dependent (AD) chromatin compartment bins are reported in the text only; their coordinates are not deposited anywhere I could find.

a1_downloadable.note: All processed files download anonymously from GEO FTP, no login or application; I fetched and parsed every one. Code is on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0. The 20-21 GB Hi-C contact maps are too large for a laptop but are not needed for the proposed task.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The three-way class (gained / lost / invariant accessibility on stimulation) IS the file identity: concatenating the 6 ATAC BED files with a class column gives the label directly. The sharper label, SATB2-dependence, needs one interval overlap between two deposited files (I ran it: 5,923 of 13,573) - effort, not construction by inference.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are mm10 genomic coordinates, not sequences. Resolving them needs ONE reference genome download (mm10.2bit, ~0.8 GB), not thousands of per-item lookups; chromosome and coordinates are present in every row.

a4_units_stated.note: Coordinates are base pairs on mm10 (build stated in Methods, not inside the files); labels are categorical so no unit ambiguity. Weakness, not a failure: the ATAC BEDs carry no signal, fold-change or FDR column, so there is no quantitative target.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted in the files: 13,573 gained + 109,573 invariant OCRs for the stimulus-response task; 5,923 SATB2-dependent vs ~6,106 SATB2-independent for the knockout-dependence task. Both far above the 1,500-row bar.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1 GB (4 MB of BED files + 0.8 GB mm10 2bit genome + cached embeddings)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified file sizes. Hi-C maps (20-21 GB) are excluded from the plan. Baseline runs on CPU with small DNA language model checkpoints; no GPU needed.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Exact matches: 13,573 gained vs 550 lost (floxed) and 11,825 lost vs 1,569 gained (knockout) in text and files; SATB2 peaks 4,552 gained and 11,068 invariant match. My recomputed overlap (5,960/11,825 = 50.4%) matches the paper's 'approximately half'. Two small discrepancies: SATB2 lost peaks are 2,042 in the file vs 2,010 in the text, and the data-availability statement swaps GSE307097 (actually CUT&Tag) with GSE307197 (actually the Hi-C files).

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels come from MACS3 peak calls on ATAC-seq reads - a physical measurement of how open DNA is to the Tn5 enzyme - not from any model's prediction, and they are independent of the DNA-sequence features a model would use. Caveat: replicates were merged before calling, so labels are thresholded calls with no per-region statistics, and they share read-depth and peak-strength confounders.

B1.why: Nine small BED files; concatenation plus one interval overlap join, which I ran successfully in the files.

B2.why: Gzipped tab-separated BED; parsed on first try with pandas, no malformed rows in 123k+ lines.

B3.why: One lab, one pipeline, but cross-genotype labels rest on separate peak calls, not a joint quantitative model.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values anywhere: just intervals and class membership, verified in files.

B5.why: Zero duplicate coordinates in all nine files; gained and invariant sets have zero overlap (I checked).

B6.why: Standard BED columns but no README; class definitions only in Methods, and GEO sample titles are mislabelled.

C1.why: Whether SATB2-dependence is locally sequence-encoded is informative either way: sequence code or 3D-context effect.

C2.why: WTKO-CNN (2026, open code) does wild-type-vs-knockout peak classification; ChromBPNet is strong but a different task.

C3.why: Nobody has modelled SATB2-dependence or activity-responsiveness in cortical neurons; clear novel plus diversity angle.

C4.why: The alternative is a mouse conditional knockout plus ATAC-seq and Hi-C: months of animal and lab work.

C5.why: Obvious dummies (majority class 49%, width, GC, SATB2-peak overlap 22.7% vs 7.1%) plus WTKO-CNN's 68-84% accuracy.

D1.why: HyenaDNA and DNABERT-2 are open-weight DNA backbones; ChromBPNet and AlphaGenome cover mouse tracks.

D2.why: Median region width 360 bp (verified), so 600-1,000 bp windows embed once on CPU and feed a simple head.

D3.why: HyenaDNA is Apache 2.0, paper is CC BY, GEO data public; nothing blocks reuse.

E1.why: Chromosome column present in every file; leave-one-chromosome-out prevents positional leakage.

E2.why: 24 chromosomes carrying 300-1,066 gained regions each, counted in the files.

E3.why: Majority class, region width alone, GC alone, promoter/distal annotation alone are all computable.

E4.why: Replicates merged before peak calling; no replicate-level calls or signal values deposited, so no noise floor.

E5.why: Must recover MEF2/AP-1 motif enrichment (paper Table S1) and the 3.2x SATB2-peak enrichment I recomputed.

E6.why: Label shuffling, width/GC-only models and SATB2-feature ablation are all trivially runnable on this table.

E7.why: GSE222609 (in vivo Satb2 knockout cortex), GSE175965 and GSE163113 (stimulated neurons) give independent held-out data.

E8.why: No published machine-learning number exists on this dataset; WTKO-CNN's numbers are on other knockouts.

G1.why: mm10 genomic coordinates with UCSC chromosome names in every row, a standard join key.

G2.why: ENCODE mouse cortex cCREs and histone ChIP (the paper already used ENCFF160SCR) join on mm10 coordinates.

G3.why: Coordinate overlap is inherently one-to-many; manageable with a summit +/-250 bp max-overlap collapse rule.

G4.why: Combination asks whether SATB2-dependent elements differ in chromatin state and transfer to in vivo cortex.

H1.why: 109,573 invariant and 11,825 knockout-lost regions give systematic negatives, counted in the files.

H2.why: One lab, one species, one culture preparation, one stimulus (bicuculline), one ATAC time point.

H3.why: The honest claim is writable in one sentence; see honest_claim_h3.

H4.why: Culture model and stimulus explicit in the paper, but replicate merging before peak calling is never flagged.

I1.why: Apostolova/Dechant lab (Innsbruck), SATB2-associated syndrome researchers, activity-dependent transcription labs.

I2.why: Would pick which elements to test in their already-deposited AAV-SATB2 rescue ATAC experiment (raw only).

I3.why: Precision in the top 100 ranked elements matches the decision: which few to test in the lab.

I4.why: A motif-count logistic regression plus SATB2-peak overlap may do nearly as well as a deep model.

J1.why: Grouped splits, frozen-backbone transfer learning, calibration, interpretation - all real modelling work.

J2.why: Motif outputs are checkable against the paper's HOMER table, but chromatin intuition would benefit from a reviewer.

J3.why: A documented mm10 table of 123k labelled OCRs with SATB2-dependence annotation is shareable even if the model is weak.

J4.why: Roughly four weeks is realistic given the small data, but no budget is written down yet.

J5.why: Kill condition stated here in success_criteria, but not yet recorded in NOTES.md with a date.

existing_models.name: WTKO-CNN (2026 arXiv preprint; 1D convolutional network with attention that classifies ATAC-seq peaks as wild-type-specific or knockout-specific)
existing_models.score_and_split: 68% accuracy (RelA, 9,886 peaks), 84% (LSD1, 1,048 peaks), 79% (EBF1, 58,955 peaks) in mouse, with chromosomes 6 and 7 held out as the test set. Accuracy only, no AUC reported.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: They attribute cross-dataset performance differences to ATAC-seq protocol variation, sample heterogeneity and the small magnitude of accessibility changes between wild-type and knockout - i.e. they have no handle on when the task is learnable.

existing_models.name: ChromBPNet (bias-factorised convolutional model predicting base-resolution chromatin accessibility from DNA sequence; Kundaje lab)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported as competitive with or better than much larger foundation models at predicting accessibility variant effects across assays, cell contexts and ancestries; evaluated on held-out genomic regions. It predicts accessibility level, not stimulus-responsiveness or knockout-dependence.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Transfer of accessibility models to perturbed or stimulated contexts; they note most stimulus-specific expression QTLs already alter chromatin in naive cells, so stimulus-specific regulatory logic remains unresolved.

existing_models.name: DeepSTARR (convolutional model predicting enhancer activity from sequence, Drosophila S2 cells)
existing_models.score_and_split: Quantitative prediction of developmental and housekeeping enhancer strength from sequence in Drosophila; held-out chromosome evaluation. Different species and no stimulus or knockout axis.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalisation of learned motif syntax to other cell types and organisms.

backbone.name: HyenaDNA-tiny-1k (open-weight DNA sequence model) with DNABERT-2 as the alternative; ChromBPNet mouse models or AlphaGenome mouse tracks as an extra feature source
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU: embed ~40,000 windows of 600-1,000 bp once, cache them, then fit logistic regression or gradient boosting heads.
backbone.licence: HyenaDNA Apache 2.0; DNABERT-2 permissive; AlphaGenome non-commercial (acceptable); data CC BY 4.0.

integration.partner_dataset: ENCODE mouse cortex/forebrain candidate cis-regulatory elements and histone ChIP-seq (the paper itself used ENCFF160SCR, ENCSR093DWU, ENCSR094TTT), plus the same group's in vivo Satb2 knockout cortex multi-omics GSE222609 (34 samples)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the activity-responsive regulatory elements that need SATB2 sit in a distinguishable pre-existing chromatin state, and does a sequence model trained on cultured neurons find the SATB2-dependent elements of intact cortex?

controls.positive_control: The model's learned features must recover the MEF2-family, FOS, JUNB, FOSL2 and NPAS4 motifs the paper's HOMER analysis found at gained OCRs, and the SATB2-binding enrichment I recomputed myself (22.7% of gained OCRs carry a SATB2 peak vs 7.1% of invariant OCRs, a 3.2-fold difference).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the SATB2-dependence labels within chromosome and confirm collapse to the majority class; train on region width alone (gained median 360 bp vs invariant 537 bp) and GC alone to quantify how much of any signal is a width/composition artifact.
controls.external_validation: GSE222609 (in vivo Satb2 conditional knockout cortex, same group, 34 samples) and GSE175965 (NPAS4:NuA4 study, 320 samples of stimulated neurons) as independently produced test sets; GSE163113 GRO-seq of KCl-stimulated neurons as a different-assay check.

honest_claim_h3: Among open chromatin regions that gain accessibility within one hour of bicuculline stimulation in cultured mouse cortical neurons from a single lab, local DNA sequence predicts which regions lose that gain when Satb2 is deleted, at a stated precision on held-out chromosomes.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the DNA sequence of gene switches that open when a neuron fires to predict which ones need the protein SATB2.
plain_idea.train_on: 13,573 short stretches of mouse genome (median 360 base pairs) that become more open within one hour of stimulating cultured cortical neurons; of these, 5,923 are labelled SATB2-dependent and about 6,106 SATB2-independent, counts I verified by intersecting the deposited files.
plain_idea.predict: A yes/no call on whether that activity-driven opening disappears when the Satb2 gene is deleted. The true answer comes from ATAC-seq, a lab assay measuring how physically open DNA is, run in Satb2 knockout versus control neurons and peak-called with MACS3.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs studying how neuronal firing switches genes on, and clinicians studying SATB2-associated syndrome, would get a ranked shortlist of switches to test in rescue experiments; even a failure tells them SATB2-dependence is not written in local sequence and must come from 3D genome context.

more_or_better_data.why: Our 13,573 activity-gained and 11,825 knockout-lost neuronal regions are comparable in size to WTKO-CNN's sets (RelA 9,886, LSD1 1,048, EBF1 58,955 peaks), but ours adds a stimulus axis none of theirs has and covers cortical pyramidal neurons, a cell type absent from their three immune/epigenetic knockouts.

confidence_score.why: The deposited files hold no replicate-level peak calls, signal values or FDRs (replicates were merged before calling, verified in the Methods and in the file columns), so per-region confidence cannot be estimated without reprocessing raw reads from the Sequence Read Archive.

models_beatable.why: WTKO-CNN is a 2026 small 1D convolutional network trained from scratch, reporting accuracy only (68-84%) with chromosomes 6 and 7 held out and no pretrained backbone; a frozen DNA language model with matched negatives and auPRC reporting is a fair step up. ChromBPNet is strong but answers a different question.

guaranteed_improvement.why: WTKO-CNN's code is public and can be retrained here as our baseline, but no existing model was ever trained on this dataset, so we cannot strictly superset its inputs; the ENCODE mouse cortex tracks that join on mm10 coordinates come from a different tissue and assay.

label_elsewhere.sources: Activity-induced accessibility change is measured in a few other published mouse neuron datasets (GSE175965 stimulated neurons, Su et al. dentate granule ATAC-seq, GSE163113 GRO-seq of KCl-stimulated neurons - all found via this paper's reference list and GEO lookups). SATB2-dependence specifically exists only here and in the same group's GSE222609.
label_elsewhere.why: A handful of independent stimulated-neuron datasets give a real external test of the activity-responsiveness half of the task, but the SATB2-dependence label has no large public counterpart, so the model cannot be validated on thousands of outside examples.

risks: Invariant regions are systematically wider than gained ones (median 537 vs 360 base pairs, verified in the files), so region width alone partly encodes the label.
The paper reports 56% of gained regions are promoter-associated, so a sequence model could learn 'promoter/CpG island' rather than 'responds to neuronal activity'.
Labels are MACS3 calls on replicate-merged libraries, so any read-depth difference between stimulated and silenced samples can create systematic calls that track GC content and mappability.
Neighbouring peaks from the same locus or repeat family can fall on both sides of a random split, inflating performance.
SATB2 binding (CUT&Tag) is both a candidate feature and close to the biological definition of SATB2-dependence, so including it can look like prediction when it is near-definition.
leakage_plan.split: Leave-one-chromosome-out over the 24 chromosomes present in the `chrom` column (I confirmed this column and its 300-1,066 gained regions per chromosome in the files), plus a WTKO-CNN-matched chr6/chr7 held-out run for comparability; before splitting, match negatives to positives on region width, GC content and promoter/distal annotation.
checks: Shuffle labels within chromosome and confirm performance collapses to the majority-class baseline.
Train on width alone, on GC alone, and on promoter/distal annotation alone, and report how much of the headline number those explain.
Measure nearest-neighbour sequence similarity (repeat-masked) between each test window and the training set, and re-score after dropping the closest matches.
Ablate the SATB2 CUT&Tag feature block and report sequence-only performance separately.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable, but only if negatives are matched on width, GC and promoter status first - unmatched negatives are the serious risk and would produce a meaningless high score.

success_criteria.metric: Area under the precision-recall curve (auPRC) for SATB2-dependence on leave-one-chromosome-out, plus precision among the top 100 ranked regions, because the user would only test a handful of elements in the lab.
success_criteria.baselines: Majority class = 49% positives (5,923 of 12,029 assignable gained regions, counted in the files); region width alone; GC alone; SATB2-peak overlap alone (22.7% of gained vs 7.1% of invariant regions, my own count); and WTKO-CNN retrained on this data, whose published accuracies are 68-84% on three other mouse knockouts.
success_criteria.success: auPRC >= 0.70 on leave-one-chromosome-out with width/GC/annotation-matched negatives, beating a confound-only model by >= 0.10 auPRC, and >= 0.60 precision in the top 100 ranked regions.
success_criteria.kill: If, after negatives are matched on width, GC and promoter/distal class, no model beats the confound-only baseline by more than 0.03 auPRC within two weeks, stop and write up the negative result.

ambitious.why: Publishes biology-first machine learning on genome regulation; would need the sequence model to predict SATB2-dependence well and to transfer to the in vivo cortex data in GSE222609.

realistic.why: Publishes careful benchmarks and modest-scope regulatory-genomics models; the likely result - sequence partly predicts activity-responsiveness, SATB2-dependence only weakly, with the confounds quantified - fits well.

fallback.journal: bioRxiv preprint plus a machine-learning-in-computational-biology workshop
fallback.why: Even a clean negative result with matched negatives and an open labelled mm10 table is worth posting, and the table itself could go to Scientific Data as a small resource.

pitch.headline: 13,573 gene switches that open when a neuron fires, of which 5,923 stop opening when one protein is deleted - a sequence-labelled table in 4 MB.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Both axes in one experiment: stimulation versus silence, and Satb2 knockout versus control, in the same cortical neuron cultures. Zero duplicate coordinates, zero overlap between the gained and invariant classes, counts matching the paper exactly.
pitch.the_win: auPRC 0.70 or better for SATB2-dependence on held-out chromosomes with width- and GC-matched negatives, against a confound-only baseline and a retrained WTKO-CNN (68-84% accuracy on other knockouts).
pitch.even_if_it_fails: A null result says SATB2-dependence is not written in local DNA sequence, so it must come from 3D genome context - which is exactly the paper's own claim, tested independently for the first time.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Apostolova/Dechant lab in Innsbruck, who already deposited AAV-SATB2 rescue ATAC-seq samples with no processed files; a ranked shortlist would tell them which elements to look at first.

ml_idea: Two nested tasks on mm10 intervals from one lab's ATAC-seq. (1) Classify open chromatin regions as activity-gained (13,573) versus invariant (109,573) in control cortical neurons from DNA sequence, using a frozen open-weight DNA backbone (HyenaDNA-tiny or DNABERT-2) plus a simple head, with negatives matched on width, GC and promoter status. (2) The distinctive task: among the 13,573 activity-gained regions, predict which are SATB2-dependent (5,923 that are lost in Satb2 knockout, verified by interval overlap) versus SATB2-independent (~6,106), with SATB2 CUT&Tag binding as a separately ablated feature block. Evaluate leave-one-chromosome-out, benchmark against WTKO-CNN retrained on the same data, and test transfer to the group's in vivo knockout cortex data (GSE222609).

effort.compute_note: BED parsing and the overlap join took under a minute on this laptop (timed). Embedding time is an estimate only: ~40,000 matched windows of 600-1,000 bp at roughly 2 sequences/second through a small DNA backbone on CPU; cross-validation time assumes cached embeddings fed to a linear or gradient-boosted head.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done: count how many activity-gained regions are SATB2-dependent (5,923 of 13,573 overlap a knockout-lost region - the label set is real and near-balanced). Next cheapest: build width/GC/promoter-matched negatives and confirm a confound-only model scores near chance; if it does not, the headline number will be an artifact.

verdict_reason: Part A verified file by file: everything downloads without login, the class label is the file identity, the counts match the paper exactly (13,573 / 550 / 1,569 / 11,825), there are no duplicates and no overlap between classes, and the labels trace to ATAC-seq measurements rather than any model's output. The distinctive task - predicting from sequence which activity-responsive elements need SATB2 - has 5,923 positives against ~6,106 negatives, which I computed myself, and no published model addresses it; the nearest one (WTKO-CNN, 2026) is a small from-scratch convolutional network reporting accuracy only. The data is 4 MB, the backbone is Apache-licensed and CPU-friendly, there is a concrete positive control (the 3.2-fold SATB2-binding enrichment I recomputed) and real external validation in the same group's in vivo data. Main risks, both testable in the first week: the gained and invariant classes differ in width and promoter content, so negatives must be matched, and a motif-count baseline may do nearly as well as a deep model.
